Alternatives to Chapter 13 include filing Chapter 7 bankruptcy to liquidate eligible unsecured debts, enrolling in a nonprofit debt management plan, negotiating debt settlements, obtaining a debt consolidation loan, or arranging direct hardship repayment plans with individual lenders.

Inside bankruptcy, the alternative is Chapter 7, whose discharge covers qualifying debts that arose before the case. Outside bankruptcy, the options are a nonprofit debt management plan, debt settlement, a consolidation loan or balance transfer, a hardship plan with each lender, or waiting out collection on protected income.

Generally yes. The IRS treats the forgiven amount as income whether or not you get a Form 1099-C, which certain creditors file when they cancel $600 or more. You can exclude it to the extent you were insolvent just before the cancellation, and debt discharged in a bankruptcy case is not taxed.

Standard consumer debt collectors cannot seize Social Security benefits deposited into your bank account. Under federal regulations, banks must automatically protect two months of direct-deposited federal benefits from account garnishment orders.

A collector must first sue you and win a judgment, according to the [CFPB](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/ask-cfpb/can-a-debt-collector-take-my-social-security-or-va-benefits-en-1157/). Even then, banks must protect two months of directly deposited federal benefits, though not benefits paid by paper check. Social Security and SSDI can sometimes be taken for government debts such as taxes and student loans or for child or spousal support, while SSI is generally protected even from those.
If you stop paying, lenders will assess late fees and penalty interest, report delinquencies to credit bureaus, and eventually charge off the debt or sell it to collection agencies.

If you stop paying, you will usually incur late fees, penalty interest and other charges. After 180 days without payment, the FTC says your creditor will write the debt off as a loss, your credit score will take a big hit, and you will still owe the debt.
